source.title: From Correlation to Cause: A Five-Stage Methodology for Feature Analysis in Transformer Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study runs activation patching on GPT-2 small using the IOI logit-difference recovery measure and tests selected canonical heads, including under prompt shifts.
record.gate_note: The study reports patching outcomes for selected heads and prompt shifts, so those are included. It does not test the complete 26-head circuit, knock out everything outside the circuit, or evaluate all seven head classes against the original faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria. Cited results from Wang et al. and baseline IOI accuracy alone are not recorded as circuit findings.
record.test_reason: The study runs per-head activation patching with the logit-difference measure on GPT-2 small IOI prompts, the original's method. It reports single-head recovery for the canonical name-mover heads and L10H7, in-distribution and under two prompt shifts. Only part of the circuit is examined.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say patching recovers the canonical IOI circuit and that head contributions are robust to all three shifts, though numbers are given only for the content-word and frame shifts. Their main claim is about SAE features: specific but partial causal force (an 'intermediate causal regime'), selectivity anticorrelated with causal force, and detection robustness diverging from causal robustness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation patching and the IOI logit-difference recovery measure, but tests selected heads at END rather than identifying and validating the full 26-head circuit against all original criteria.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies prompt distribution: content words are replaced and the prompt frame is reformulated. It reports selected-head recovery as essentially unchanged under these conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating 15 name-selective SAE features at L9 END cuts logit difference only from +3.71 to +3.33, with 98.4% of prompts still correct. Single-feature ablation effects halve under the cleft frame while the features still fire.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: IOI-relevant information at the name-mover site is distributed and redundant across SAE features, and feature causal force is less robust to prompt shifts than feature detection.

record.problems: Patching is reported for selected heads and uses 30 minimal pairs for the initial head analysis; the study gives no uncertainty estimates. It does not test the complete circuit, outside-circuit knockout, or the original faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported selected-head patching outcomes were left out. The study's SAE-feature ablations and monitoring results were not recorded as circuit rows because they do not test the attention-head circuit.

untested.parts: Per-head patching covers only the name-mover heads at END and L10H7. Not tested: duplicate-token, induction and S-inhibition heads individually, the full 26-head set, knockout of everything outside the circuit, and the faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria. S-inhibition is claimed only qualitatively from the residual-stream sweep.
No main name-mover heads are ablated, and takeover by other heads is not measured.
No other models, sizes, checkpoints or tasks.
No alternative circuit-finding methods, ablation types or metrics are compared.
Circuit faithfulness and completeness are never computed under any ablation, metric or distribution. The SAE-feature findings concern features, not the head circuit.
Head-patching results are not separated by ABBA/BABA order. No numbers are given for held-out names, and more than two names are not tested.

missing.what: Residual-stream patching sweep over layers × positions, which the authors cite as showing the S-inhibition signature (negative recovery at the S position in early layers).

Authors claim the circuit is robust to all three shifts, including held-out names, but give no head-recovery numbers for held-out names. Figure 7a shows only in-distribution, OOD content and new frame.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'challenges' label is removed. Stable single-head recovery across prompts does not measure circuit faithfulness or completeness, so V5 is untested. L10H7 is mislabelled 'backup' by the authors; Wang et al. call it a negative name mover. Weaknesses: n=30 pairs, no uncertainty estimates, single author, preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests selected canonical heads with patching, but not the full 26-head, seven-class circuit, the knockout of everything outside it, or its faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria.
It reports negative recovery for a backup head but does not ablate main name-mover heads or test whether other heads take over.
No other models, sizes, checkpoints, or task reuse are tested.
No alternative circuit-finding methods, ablation types, or metrics are compared.

The study compares selected-head patching under prompt shifts, but does not compare ablation types or establish circuit completeness. Its SAE-feature ablations are not tests of the attention-head circuit.
The study tests selected-head patching under content-word changes and one reformulated frame. It does not report head-patching results separated by name order or on held-out names.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small, canonical IOI template, per-head patching at END, n=30 pairs
relationships.reason: L9H9, L9H6 and L10H0 give the largest positive recoveries and L10H7 a strong negative one, matching the name-mover and negative name-mover roles (r1–r4). Only these head classes are tested.
relationships.display_finding: L9H9, L9H6 and L10H0 produced the largest positive recoveries, while L10H7 produced a strong negative recovery, matching their proposed name-mover roles.
